nodes.title: Reporting and documentation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Reporting questions appear in PenTest+, CySA+, and SOC analyst tracks. Findings are only valuable if stakeholders can act on them — structure, audience, severity scoring, and remediation guidance are what separate junior from senior write-ups.

flashcards.front: What's the standard pentest report structure?
flashcards.back: Executive summary (1-2 pages, no jargon, business impact). Methodology (scope, dates, tools, tester names). Findings (one per vuln, with CVSS, evidence screenshots, repro steps). Recommendations (specific, prioritized). Appendix (raw scan output, tool versions, IP lists). The exec summary is the only part C-levels read — make it stand alone.

Common Vulnerability Scoring System: 0-10 severity score combining exploitability and impact metrics. 9.0-10.0 = Critical, 7.0-8.9 = High, 4.0-6.9 = Medium. Use it to prioritize fixes — but adjust for YOUR environment (a critical RCE behind a firewall in a dev VLAN may be lower business risk than a medium XSS on the login page).

flashcards.front: Who's the audience for each report section?
flashcards.back: Exec summary: CISO / CTO / board — business impact only. Findings detail: developers and sysadmins — needs every CVE, command, and IP. Methodology: legal and audit — proves you stayed in scope. Tailor language and depth per audience; one giant report with everything pleases no one.

flashcards.front: Why include remediation guidance, not just findings?
flashcards.back: A report that says 'SQL injection on /login' without 'use parameterized queries with these examples' makes the dev guess. Generic findings get ignored. Specific remediation with code snippets and reference links (OWASP, vendor docs) is what makes the gap actually close. Pentest is half offense, half teaching.

questions.q: An IS auditor must conclude on the operating effectiveness of an access-review control across a full year. Which sampling approach provides the BEST statistical basis for projecting results to the population?
choices: Judgmental sampling of high-risk users only
Sampling only the first and last month of the year
Sampling whichever review records the system owner provides
Statistical (random) sampling sized to the desired confidence and precision
questions.explanation: Only statistical sampling lets the auditor extrapolate results to the population with measurable confidence and precision — exactly what is needed to conclude on operating effectiveness over a full period. Judgmental sampling is not projectable; period-end-only sampling misses interim failures; and relying on management's selection introduces bias and breaches auditor independence.

questions.q: An IS auditor must conclude on the integrity of a financial application's transaction log. Which evidence is the MOST reliable?
choices: A signed letter from the application owner confirming the log is intact
Hash values produced by an independent forensic tool comparing two snapshots
A screenshot taken by the developer showing recent transactions
A verbal walkthrough from the database administrator
questions.explanation: ISACA ranks evidence by independence and objectivity: independently computed hash values produced by a tool outside the audited party's control sit at the top of the hierarchy. Owner letters, developer screenshots and DBA walkthroughs are all representations from interested parties and can be selectively prepared, so they carry materially lower reliability.

questions.q: An IS audit manager with limited resources is drafting the annual audit plan and must decide which engagements to include from a large audit universe. Engagement selection should be based PRIMARILY on:
choices: Areas where the auditee has explicitly requested coverage
The IS audit team's familiarity with the technology in scope
A documented IT risk assessment ranking auditable units
Whatever areas were covered in the prior-year plan, for continuity
questions.explanation: ISACA's standards require the annual plan to be risk-based, with engagements prioritised against a current, documented IT risk assessment of the auditable universe. Auditee preference, prior-year coverage and auditor comfort all skew the plan away from the highest-risk areas and toward what is convenient rather than what matters most.

questions.q: An IS auditor is planning the annual audit universe and must decide where to focus limited hours. Which approach is MOST appropriate for prioritizing which systems to audit?
choices: Audit the systems that were audited least recently, to ensure even coverage over time.
Use a risk-based approach that ranks auditable areas by the significance of the risk to business objectives.
Audit whichever systems the CIO nominates as most important to the business.
Rotate through every system alphabetically so nothing is ever skipped.
questions.explanation: A risk-based audit plan allocates scarce audit resources to the areas of greatest risk to the organization's objectives — the professional standard for audit planning. Auditing by recency, by management nomination, or alphabetically ignores where the real exposure lies; management input is one factor but cannot replace an independent risk assessment, and even coverage is not the goal — proportionate coverage of risk is.

questions.q: During fieldwork an auditor discovers a control deficiency that management strongly disputes. What should the auditor do FIRST?
choices: Corroborate the finding with sufficient and appropriate evidence and discuss it with management before finalizing.
Escalate immediately to the audit committee before discussing it with management.
Remove the finding from the report to preserve the working relationship with management.
Report the deficiency to the external regulator as a compliance breach.
questions.explanation: An auditor must support every finding with sufficient, appropriate evidence and validate it with management before it is reported, giving management the chance to provide context or correct a misunderstanding. Deleting a supported finding compromises independence, jumping straight to the audit committee or a regulator skips due process, and premature external reporting is inappropriate before the finding is even substantiated.

nodes.title: Protection Of Assets: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Protection Of Assets. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A corporate laptop containing customer records is stolen from an employee's car. Which control would have BEST limited the data exposure?
flashcards.back: Once a device is physically in attacker hands, only cryptographic protection of the data at rest meaningfully limits exposure: full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication keeps the contents unreadable without the key. BIOS passwords are trivially bypassed by removing the disk, the AUP is an administrative control with no protective effect against a thief, and antivirus addresses malware on a running system rather than physical loss.

flashcards.front: An IS auditor reviewing user access in a financial system finds that 18 terminated employees retain active accounts up to 90 days after their departure. The BEST recommendation is to:
flashcards.back: The root cause is a process gap between HR and identity management. The strongest fix drives deactivation from the authoritative HR system, so terminations close access immediately and consistently. Quarterly certifications and manager emails are compensating controls that still leave gaps measured in weeks or months, and extending log retention has no preventive effect on the access remaining active.

flashcards.front: A financial reporting application is reachable from the public internet using only a username and password. Which control would MOST effectively reduce the risk of account compromise?
flashcards.back: Credential phishing and password reuse defeat any password-only scheme regardless of length or rotation. Multi-factor authentication with a phishing-resistant factor (for example FIDO2 security keys) breaks the attack chain even when the password is known to the attacker. Frequent rotation actually weakens password quality in practice, raw length still falls to phishing, and time-based restrictions are trivially circumvented by attackers operating from another time zone.

flashcards.front: An auditor reviews a firm's data-retention practices and finds emails are kept indefinitely 'just in case.' What is the main risk the auditor should raise?
flashcards.back: Keeping data longer than needed raises cost, expands the e-discovery surface in litigation, and can violate data-minimization and privacy regulations. The auditor should recommend a defined retention schedule aligned to legal and regulatory requirements, with defensible disposal. Indefinite retention is not a strength, the issue is far more than backup speed, and retention has clear legal/compliance implications beyond IT.

questions.q: A corporate laptop containing customer records is stolen from an employee's car. Which control would have BEST limited the data exposure?
choices: A strong BIOS password protecting the boot sequence
A signed acceptable-use policy acknowledged by the user at hire
Antivirus software with up-to-date signature definitions
Full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication
questions.explanation: Once a device is physically in attacker hands, only cryptographic protection of the data at rest meaningfully limits exposure: full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication keeps the contents unreadable without the key. BIOS passwords are trivially bypassed by removing the disk, the AUP is an administrative control with no protective effect against a thief, and antivirus addresses malware on a running system rather than physical loss.

questions.q: An IS auditor reviewing user access in a financial system finds that 18 terminated employees retain active accounts up to 90 days after their departure. The BEST recommendation is to:
choices: Integrate the joiner-mover-leaver process with HR so departures trigger automatic account deactivation
Run a quarterly access certification campaign covering all users in the system
Require managers to email the IT helpdesk whenever a member of their team leaves
Lengthen the audit log retention period so missed departures can still be detected later
questions.explanation: The root cause is a process gap between HR and identity management. The strongest fix drives deactivation from the authoritative HR system, so terminations close access immediately and consistently. Quarterly certifications and manager emails are compensating controls that still leave gaps measured in weeks or months, and extending log retention has no preventive effect on the access remaining active.

questions.q: A financial reporting application is reachable from the public internet using only a username and password. Which control would MOST effectively reduce the risk of account compromise?
choices: Forcing users to change their passwords every 30 days
Increasing the minimum password length to 16 characters
Requiring multi-factor authentication using a phishing-resistant factor
Restricting interactive logins to local business hours only
questions.explanation: Credential phishing and password reuse defeat any password-only scheme regardless of length or rotation. Multi-factor authentication with a phishing-resistant factor (for example FIDO2 security keys) breaks the attack chain even when the password is known to the attacker. Frequent rotation actually weakens password quality in practice, raw length still falls to phishing, and time-based restrictions are trivially circumvented by attackers operating from another time zone.

questions.q: An auditor reviews a firm's data-retention practices and finds emails are kept indefinitely 'just in case.' What is the main risk the auditor should raise?
choices: Over-retention increases storage cost and legal/e-discovery exposure and may breach data-minimization requirements; retention should follow a defined, legally-informed schedule.
Indefinite retention improves security and should be commended.
The only issue is that backups will run slightly slower.
Retention length is purely an IT decision with no compliance dimension.
questions.explanation: Keeping data longer than needed raises cost, expands the e-discovery surface in litigation, and can violate data-minimization and privacy regulations. The auditor should recommend a defined retention schedule aligned to legal and regulatory requirements, with defensible disposal. Indefinite retention is not a strength, the issue is far more than backup speed, and retention has clear legal/compliance implications beyond IT.

questions.q: A CISA is assessing a newly deployed application's user access. Which test provides the STRONGEST evidence that access rights match policy?
choices: Ask the system administrator whether access is configured correctly.
Re-perform a sample by comparing actual system entitlements against approved access requests and job roles.
Review the access-request policy document for completeness.
Confirm that a firewall protects the application server.
questions.explanation: Re-performance — independently comparing what the system actually grants against documented approvals and job roles — yields the strongest, most reliable audit evidence. Inquiry (asking the admin) is the weakest form of evidence, reviewing the policy tests design not operation, and a firewall check addresses network exposure, not whether user entitlements match policy.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An IS auditor reviews the newly formed IT steering committee's charter to assess whether the committee is positioned to align IT with business strategy. Which committee composition BEST supports IT governance objectives?
choices: Senior business executives, the CIO and the CFO, chaired by a business executive
Only the CIO, CTO and head of infrastructure operations
The CIO and a rotating group of project managers from active initiatives
The CEO alone, making all IT investment decisions on the committee's behalf
questions.explanation: Effective IT governance demands that IT investments be steered by the business. A committee that includes senior business executives alongside the CIO and CFO — and is chaired by a business leader rather than the CIO — keeps decisions tied to business value and risk appetite. An IT-only committee biases decisions toward technology, project managers operate at delivery level, and CEO-only decision-making bypasses the deliberative review the committee is meant to provide.

questions.q: A small organization has too few staff to fully segregate database administration from application development, and management asks the auditor how to reduce the resulting risk. Which compensating control is MOST effective?
choices: Requiring the DBA to take annual mandatory leave
Rotating the DBA role between two staff every six months
Independent review of DBA activity logs with alerting on privileged actions
Increasing the password complexity requirements for the DBA account
questions.explanation: When segregation of duties is infeasible, the strongest compensating control is detective: an independent reviewer monitors the privileged user's activity logs with alerts on sensitive actions, so misuse is detected promptly. Mandatory leave and role rotation are periodic and miss anything done between cycles, and password complexity does nothing to constrain an authorised privileged user.

questions.q: A company grants developers standing access to modify code directly in production 'for emergencies.' From a controls standpoint, what is the primary concern and the best compensating control if the access cannot be removed immediately?
choices: The concern is performance; the compensating control is faster hardware.
The concern is a segregation-of-duties violation; the compensating control is detailed, independent review of all production changes via logged, monitored activity.
The concern is licensing cost; the compensating control is an audit of software licenses.
There is no concern because developers understand the code best.
questions.explanation: Developers with unrestricted production access breach segregation of duties — the same people who write code should not be able to move it into production unchecked, which enables both error and fraud. When the access cannot be revoked at once, the standard compensating control is independent detective review: all production changes are logged and monitored, and an independent party reviews them. Performance, licensing, and 'they know best' miss the control risk entirely.

questions.q: An organisation has set an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 4 hours for its order-entry system. Which strategy MOST efficiently meets BOTH objectives?
choices: Hourly transaction log shipping plus a warm standby server at the DR site
Nightly tape backups shipped offsite each morning
Weekly full backups stored on a local NAS in the production data centre
Quarterly snapshots replicated to a second rack in the same data centre
questions.explanation: A 1-hour RPO requires data to be replicated at least hourly, and a 4-hour RTO requires infrastructure that can be brought online comfortably within that window. Hourly log shipping satisfies the RPO and a warm standby satisfies the RTO. Nightly tapes already blow the RPO by up to 24 hours, weekly NAS backups blow it further, and same-data-centre snapshots violate site-diversity requirements for credible DR.

questions.q: An auditor is evaluating whether an organization's backup strategy will actually work when a real disaster strikes rather than merely on paper. The MOST important indicator that the backup strategy will succeed during a real disaster is:
choices: The number of backup jobs that report a "success" status each night
The total capacity of the offsite media library
Documented evidence of successful periodic restore tests against defined objectives
The strength of the encryption algorithm used on the backup media
questions.explanation: A "success" status only confirms a job ran — organisations regularly discover at recovery time that the resulting backups were unreadable, partial or missing critical data. ISACA emphasises that only documented, successful restore tests against the stated RPO and RTO actually prove recoverability. Library capacity and encryption strength are useful operational concerns but say nothing about whether the data can be brought back.

questions.q: An organization's disaster-recovery plan specifies an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes for a core database. Which recovery strategy BEST meets both targets?
choices: Nightly full backups shipped to offsite tape storage.
Weekly backups with a cold standby site provisioned on demand.
Manual re-keying of transactions from paper records after an outage.
Asynchronous replication to a warm site with frequent transaction-log shipping.
questions.explanation: An RPO of 15 minutes means at most 15 minutes of data loss, and an RTO of 4 hours means recovery within 4 hours — a warm site with frequent log shipping/near-real-time replication meets both. Nightly or weekly backups leave hours-to-days of data loss (RPO fail), a cold site provisioned on demand rarely restores within 4 hours (RTO fail), and manual re-keying satisfies neither and is error-prone.

questions.q: An IS auditor is engaged during the design phase of a new application. The auditor's PRIMARY role is to:
choices: Take responsibility for designing the application's internal controls
Approve the final design before construction work may begin
Develop the test scripts that will be executed during user acceptance testing
Assess whether the proposed controls will adequately address identified risks
questions.explanation: ISACA stresses auditor independence: the auditor advises and assesses but does not own control design, approve solutions or write tests, because any of those activities would create a self-review conflict at later audit. The proper role during design is to provide independent assurance that the proposed controls map to the documented risks the project is meant to mitigate.

questions.q: An IS auditor participates in a project as an advisor during system development. At the post-implementation review, what is the primary threat to the auditor's objectivity?
choices: The auditor may lack technical knowledge of the new system.
The auditor will not have access to production logs.
The auditor could be reviewing controls they themselves recommended, creating a self-review / independence impairment.
The project team may finish the system late.
questions.explanation: When an auditor advises on control design and later audits those same controls, they end up reviewing their own work — a self-review threat that impairs independence and objectivity. This must be disclosed and, ideally, the post-implementation review assigned to a different auditor. Technical familiarity, log access, and schedule slippage are project concerns, not the core independence issue.
